newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt markets end weaker after choppy day.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt markets end weaker after choppy day.

text.p: 0500 GMT
* NZ yields end slightly higher after whippy session
* Strong retail sales gives little lasting impetus
* Bond dealers watch spreads to offshore widening
* Cash at 10.00 pct vs 10.00 pct at Monday's close
* 90 day bills 9.89 pct vs 9.86 pct
* 7/98 bond yields 8.14 pct vs 8.11 pct
* 02/01 bond yields 8.35 pct vs 8.32 pct
* 11/06 bond yields 8.38 pct vs 8.35 pct
* Dec bank bill futures 90.63 vs 90.64, vol 1,492
New Zealand debt markets ended slightly weaker on Tuesday after a choppy trading session.
Money market dealers said statistics showing seasonally adjusted retail sales climbing a strong 2.3 percent in July were largely in line with expectations, although the market sold off initially.
The rise follows a fall of 3.2 percent in June.
One dealer said the strength of the sales data came as no real surprise given that credit card billings and consumer confidence were up in July.
Physical bank bills ended three points weaker, on their opening level of 9.89 percent. Futures had a fairly active day, with 1,492 contracts traded, but finished steady at 90.63.
The front contracts were seen torn between support around 90.59-60 and resistance at 90.65-66, and went nowhere at the end of the day.
One bond dealer said sentiment continued to deteriorate, with all the action elsewhere and New Zealand yields moving only slightly higher on the day.
"In an absolute sense not much is happening. But in a relative sense quite significant things are happening.
"All the offshore bond markets are basically pretty strong...but this local market is going backwards," he said.
The spread against U.S. three-year Treasuries has widened to 209 points from around 180 at the end of August, and to 129 from 100 over the Australian three-year bonds.
"We're finally getting in a bit of insurance against the election, but we're getting it by going half a step backwards while everyone else takes two steps forward."
New Zealand will hold its first general election under a new Mixed Member Proportional (MMP) voting system on October 12. The system is conducive to minority or coalition governments.
The dealer said the local market, after a period of optimism, now seemed to believe the governing National Party would not play a major role in the post-election line-up.
-- Catherine McCaw (64 4) 471 4275
